Jesus knew that he was about to be put to death. Before that happened, he spent time praying. Jesus’ prayer showed the close relationship between Jesus and his Father. He prayed first about the many things he shares with his Father. They share glory, authority, eternal life and their work.

Next Jesus prayed for his disciples. He asked God to keep them safe in a world that is full of hate. Jesus prayed for their relationships with one another. He wanted them to be one as he and the Father are one. He also wanted them to be full of his joy.

Then Jesus prayed for all who would follow him in the future. Jesus wants his followers to be joined together as one by their love for him. Jesus talked about how this helps the world. He was talking about people in the world who don’t know him yet. It helps them understand how much God loves them. When Jesus’ followers disagree about who he is, others don’t learn to know Jesus. It makes it hard for others to trust Jesus’ words. Jesus is eager to share his glory and his love with all who trust in him.
T

This chapter contains the longest prayer of Jesus. People often refer to it as the "high priestly prayer." The prayer shows the deepest concerns and purposes of Jesus. 

This prayer concludes his last words that began at {{John 13:31|13:31}}. Jesus expressed his own concerns to his Father ({{John 17:1-8|17:1–8}}). He then expressed concerns for the church and its future ({{John 17:9-26|17:9–26}}).
T
All authority has been placed in Jesus’ hands ({{John 3:35|3:35}}); he can give eternal life as only God can ({{John 3:15|3:15}}; {{John 5:21|5:21}}, {{John 5:25-26|25–26}}).
T

- *that they may know you*: In the Hebrew language, "knowing" includes experience and intimacy. For Christians, this means loving God and obeying him. 

- *whom You have sent*: Jesus came from heaven and was returning ({{John 17:5|John 17:5}}). So he has divine authority as God's agent.
T
The miracles of Jesus displayed God's glory to the world ({{John 1:14|1:14}}). This task was finished. The life and obedience of Jesus glorified God.
T
Jesus prayed to return to the position he had with God before the world began ({{John 1:1|1:1}}).
T

This verse summarizes what Jesus came to do. He revealed the true person of God to the world, gathered up God’s people into his flock, and instructed them in obedience. The result of this work is the church.
T
Jesus revealed himself to the world. Those who received his message became children of God ({{John 1:12|1:12}}; {{John 11:52|11:52}}). He revealed God's word to them.
T
Jesus prayed for his disciples, who must continue his work after his departure.
T

Just as the Son brings glory to the Father ({{John 17:1|17:1}}, {{John 17:4-5|4–5}}), the disciples bring the Son glory ({{John 17:22|17:22}}). The love and obedience that brought glory to God in the life of Jesus become features of his disciples’ lives.
T
The first concern Jesus had for his disciples was that they would remain united with each other in the same way he is one with the Father.
T

Until now, Jesus had guarded his followers. Now he was concerned for their strength and survival in his absence, because the world would be hostile toward them and their mission of challenging the world by preaching the truth ({{John 15:18-27|15:18–27}}; {{John 16:8-11|16:8–11}}). After Jesus departed to heaven, the Holy Spirit would protect them and bring them joy ({{John 15:26|15:26}}).
T

God’s word, which Jesus had given his disciples, also provides a defense against the world. The Spirit would preserve and recall God’s word in the church ({{John 14:26|14:26}}), equipping the church for its encounter with the world.
T

*Sanctify*: This refers to purity gained by separation from the world, and living a life so aligned with God that it reflects Disciples are set apart by God, equipped by the Spirit, and prepared by God’s word to enter the world without being victimized by its darkness.
T

*I sanctify Myself*: Priests and prophets were similarly set apart for service to God ({{Leviticus 8:30|Leviticus 8:30}}; {{Jeremiah 1:5|Jeremiah 1:5}}). Jesus again committed himself to God's mission. He recognized that he was set apart for the purpose of the cross. The disciples would benefit because his death would enable them to experience new holiness in a deep attachment to God.
T

Jesus was praying for other sheep who were not yet in his flock ({{John 10:16|10:16}}). These are the believers through the centuries who have come to faith through the witness of the disciples of Jesus.
T

- *Be one*: For believers, becoming one with one another is an outgrowth of the union they enjoy with Jesus himself, a union modeled on the oneness of the Father and the Son. 

- *May they also be in Us*: Through the Holy Spirit's power, believers experience a profound and intimate union with the Father and the Son, leading to transformation ({{John 14:20|14:20}}, {{John 14:23|23}}; {{1 John 4:13|1 John 4:13}}).

- Disciples of Jesus represent him, so their right actions and relationships with each other reflect the credibility of Christ in the world. When there is disunity, infighting, and intolerance, their testimony to the world is unconvincing. When people observe the community of believers, they know that it represents Jesus; a unified, loving community convinces the world to believe ({{John 13:35|John 13:35}}; {{1 John 3:11|1 John 3:11}}).
T
The community of believers should display the same glory that Jesus displayed from the Father.
T
*so that the world may know*: If the church lives in the Spirit, reflects God’s glory and love, and shows unity sustained by a shared knowledge of God, then its testimony will amaze the world.
T

I want those You have given Me to be with Me: Someday, all the followers of Jesus will see his true glory and the love that has existed in heaven before the beginning of time ({{John 17:5|17:5}}). Jesus was returning to heaven and deeply wanted to see his disciples there so that they might witness what words on earth cannot describe.
T

- All who accept the Son and embrace the Father will experience the kind of love known only between the Father and the Son. 

- *I in them*: Jesus loves his followers and wants to fill them with glory and joy that compares to nothing in the world.
T

- Jesus crossed the Kidron Valley. This was a dry river valley (a wadi) outside the eastern walls of Jerusalem. 

- *a garden*: This is the Garden of Gethsemane ({{Mark 14:32|Mark 14:32}}). This garden was a group of olive trees on the west side of the Mount of Olives. The Aramaic name *gath shemaney* means “olive press.” Jesus liked this place and often prayed there (see {{John 8:1|John 8:1}}; {{Luke 21:37|Luke 21:37}}; {{Luke 22:39|22:39}}).
B

This was the same night that John wrote about in chapter 13. It was the night when Jesus had shared his last meal with the 12 disciples.

Jesus had washed Judas’ feet even though Judas wouldn’t be a faithful friend to him. Judas knew where to find Jesus that night. He led the soldiers and officials to the garden and handed Jesus over to them.

Jesus spoke about himself as I am. The soldiers and officials were shocked when Jesus did that. This was because God had used those words to describe himself (Exodus 3:14).

The other 11 disciples were confused about what was happening. They thought that Jesus’ battle was against human beings. So Peter tried to protect Jesus by using violence. No one understood that Jesus was fighting a battle against sin and death.

Jesus was choosing to obey his Father. He was willing to suffer to bring eternal life to the world.
T

Jesus finished speaking his final words to his disciples in the upper room ({{John 13:31-17:26|13:31–17:26}}). Jesus then left the city and went to a garden east of Jerusalem to pray. There, authorities arrested him and took him back into the city for questioning by the Jewish religious leaders. The important "hour" Jesus often mentioned throughout the Gospel had arrived (see {{John 2:4|2:4}}; see also study note on 12:23).
T

John’s full account of the group that arrested him adds details not mentioned in the other Gospels. The temple authorities sent Roman soldiers and temple guards. While the temple guards arrested Jesus, the Roman soldiers stood by to prevent a riot. The Roman group was large enough to need a commander. They came with weapons and were expecting a struggle ({{John 18:10|18:10,}}{{John 18:12|12}}). Many people claimed to be the Messiah. Often, they tried to force the Romans out of the land, which caused political conflict.
T

*I am He* (literally *I am*): Jesus identified himself by the divine name God had revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai (see {{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}; see also {{John 4:26|John 4:26}}; {{John 8:24|8:24}}, {{John 8:58|58}}).
T

All the soldiers and guards fell back before the Lord (compare {{Isaiah 6:5|Isaiah 6:5}}; {{Ezekiel 1:28|Ezekiel 1:28}}; {{Daniel 10:9|Daniel 10:9}}; {{Acts 9:4|Acts 9:4}}; {{Revelation 1:17|Revelation 1:17}}). Even the Roman soldiers, who were trained to stand firm, fell to the ground before Christ. They did this to show submission, but they did not fully understand what had happened and went on with the arrest.
T
*I am He*: Jesus used God's divine name for the second time (see study note on 18:5).
T

*I have not lost one*: Jesus continued to be a good shepherd, offering his life for the sheep and protecting them from the wolves ({{John 10:11-15|10:11–15}}). From the beginning, however, Judas Iscariot had not been a true disciple of Jesus ({{John 17:12|17:12}}).
T

- *Simon Peter drew his sword*: This was a short sword or long knife, usually worn with everyday clothes.

- The Hebrew name *Malchus* means "king." John may have included this detail as a subtle wordplay pointing to the true identity of Jesus (see {{John 18:36-37|18:36–37}}; {{John 19:19|19:19}}).

- *Put your sword back*: The mission of Jesus was not to fight for his life, but to die for ours.
T

- Soldiers bound Jesus and took him back to Jerusalem. 

- First, they brought him to Annas, who had been the high priest and remained very influential. Five of his sons also became high priests. Caiaphas, his son-in-law, was the official high priest at that time (see {{John 18:24|18:24}}).
B

Two trials went on at the same time. First, Israel’s religious leaders put Jesus on trial as a false teacher. That would give them the right to put Jesus to death (Deuteronomy 13:5). Yet John’s gospel had shown that Jesus wasn’t a false teacher. Everything Jesus taught came from the Father himself.

Second, Peter was on trial in a different way. Was he a follower of Jesus? He went with Jesus to his trial before the high priest. This could have been dangerous for Peter. In John’s gospel, many who believed in Jesus were afraid to say so in public. Those who were openly committed to him faced many kinds of trouble. So when people asked Peter if he was Jesus’ disciple, he said he wasn’t. Peter had often shown strong faith in Jesus. Yet at that important moment he allowed fear to control him. Jesus’ friends left him. Jesus would be alone as he finished the work his Father had given him to do.
T

*one man died for the people*: Caiaphas had said this as a political calculation ({{John 11:49-50|11:49–50}}). John points out the irony: the death of Jesus did not bring political freedom to Israel. Instead, it brought spiritual salvation for everyone who believes in him.
T
*another disciple*: The other disciple is not named but was probably "the one whom Jesus loved" ({{John 13:23|13:23}}). This disciple was the apostle John and the author of this book.
T

While Annas was questioning Jesus, the girl watching the door asked Peter if he was one of the disciples of Jesus ({{John 18:12-14|18:12–14}}, {{John 18:19-24|19–24}}). Jesus confronted his questioners and denied nothing. But Peter quickly denied his connection to Jesus three times ({{John 18:17|18:17}}, {{John 18:25|25}}, {{John 18:27|27}}).
T

The high priest asked Jesus questions, which went against Jewish legal procedures. In Jewish court, the priest did not directly question the person on the defense. Instead, they gathered evidence from witnesses to prove guilt (see {{Numbers 35:30|Numbers 35:30}}; {{Deuteronomy 17:6|Deuteronomy 17:6}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:15|19:15}}; compare {{Matthew 18:16|Matthew 18:16}}). If Jesus said anything that would make him guilty, Annas would use it against him at his trial. Annas tried to follow Roman practice by making Jesus say something about himself that would make him guilty. This was different than using witnesses as Jewish law required.
T
Jesus's direct response reminded Annas that everything was public knowledge. This exposed the priest's attempt to follow Roman practice.
T

When Jesus reminded Annas about the correct legal procedure, one of the temple guards thought he was being disrespectful. The guard slapped Jesus.

However, Jesus knew the law well and spoke truthfully. There were no witnesses accusing him, and no evidence was presented against him.
T
Annas could say no more. His questioning had failed. So he sent Jesus to Caiaphas to be tried before the Sanhedrin, Jerusalem's judicial high council (see {{Mark 14:53-15:1|Mark 14:53–15:1}}).
T
*He denied it*: Peter *denied* knowing Jesus three times. Later, Jesus asked Peter three times to reaffirm his love ({{John 21:15-17|21:15–17}}).
T

- The trial before Caiaphas ended in the early hours of the morning. The Sanhedrin (Jewish high council) did not have the power to execute someone. They needed Pilate, the Roman governor, to carry out an execution ({{John 18:31|18:31}}). 

- They did not want to become ritually unclean by contact with Gentiles in Pilate’s headquarters. So Pilate, probably fearing a riot, went outside to meet them. 

- The Passover meal itself had taken place the night before (see {{John 13:1|13:1}}; {{Mark 14:14-16|Mark 14:14–16}}). The next day, another meal began the week-long Feast of Unleavened Bread ({{Leviticus 23:5-6|Leviticus 23:5–6}}).
B

The Jewish leaders moved Jesus to the palace of the Roman governor Pilate.

The Roman government didn’t want any Jew to claim that he was Israel’s true king. Jewish messiahs who claimed to be king would lead armed groups to attack the government. The Romans would put them to death on a cross. So the Jewish leaders charged Jesus with claiming to be a king.

Pilate and Jesus talked about being king, about power and about truth. Pilate couldn’t understand what Jesus was talking about. Jesus is indeed the King. He is King of Israel and of the world. But his kingdom isn’t like human governments. Jesus’ kingdom is God’s kingdom and it’s based on truth and on love.

Jesus was showing God’s love as he was on trial. He was giving up his life to set others free. The crowd asked Pilate to set Barabbas free from prison instead of Jesus.
T

Pilate, the fifth Roman governor of Judea, ruled the country from AD 26 to 36. He usually lived on the coast in Caesarea, but kept troops stationed in a fortress in Jerusalem where he appeared personally for major festivals. He was a brutal ruler whose atrocities against the Jews were legendary (for example, {{Luke 13:1|Luke 13:1}}; Josephus, *War* 2.9.2–4).
T

Pilate did not consider the charges convincing. So he told the Sanhedrin to judge Jesus by their own law. Pilate saw this as a Jewish argument, which he refused to investigate. 

However, the Jewish leaders insisted that execution was necessary. This fulfilled the prediction Jesus made about how he would die (see {{John 12:32-33|12:32–33}}). The Jews would have used stoning, but the Romans used crucifixion. If Pilate sentenced Jesus, the Romans would hang Jesus on a cross to die.
T

- Pilate was personally responsible for capital crimes in which the interests and security of the Roman Empire were at stake, so he began his formal legal inquiry.

- *Are You the King of the Jews?*: To get the governor’s attention, Caiaphas accused Jesus of telling people not to pay taxes to Rome and claiming to be a king ({{Luke 23:2|Luke 23:2}}). To Pilate, Jesus might have seemed like another Jewish terrorist or revolutionary with ideas about the Messiah and a group of armed followers (see {{Luke 23:18-19|Luke 23:18–19}}; {{Acts 5:36-37|Acts 5:36–37}}).
T

The response Jesus gave forced the governor to reveal the origin of his question. The temple leaders were responsible for these accusations. Pilate only wanted to know if Jesus was a rebel who might threaten Roman interests.
T

Jesus was willing to accept the title of king, but he made it clear that he did not govern an earthly kingdom that might rival Rome. The kingship of Jesus is not of this world. Rather than being a political ruler, he rules through the devotion and obedience of his followers.
T

- *What is truth?*: Truth was not a foreign idea to Pilate. But he did not wait for an answer because he did not believe there was one. 

- Pilate returned to the council members waiting outside and delivered his verdict: not guilty. Although he referred to Jesus as “King of the Jews” (see also {{John 19:19|19:19}}), the title was just an expression meant to mock Jesus. Pilate wanted to release Jesus. His offer showed that he did not want Jesus to be executed.
T

Jesus was not a threat to Rome, but Barabbas was a revolutionary. He was a violent man involved in political uprisings. Barabbas had proven his capacity to challenge the Roman military occupation of Israel (see {{Luke 23:19|Luke 23:19}}).
B

Pilate allowed the soldiers to treat Jesus badly. They made fun of Jesus and hurt him.

Pilate knew that the charges against Jesus were false. He was confused about who Jesus was. Pilate thought that he had power and authority over Jesus. He believed he could choose whether to put Jesus to death or set him free.

Jesus explained that Pilate only had as much power as God allowed him to have. Then the Jewish leaders talked about Caesar’s power as king. Pilate was afraid. He wanted to set Jesus free but he allowed him to be put to death.

Israel’s leaders said that their king was Caesar. This meant that they didn’t accept either Jesus or God as their King. They were saying a clear and final no to God. This was very sad.
T

Pilate had Jesus beaten after his sentencing ({{Mark 15:15|Mark 15:15}}). However, John here describes an earlier beating. This was likely Pilate's attempt to show that Jesus had been punished and he could release him ({{John 19:4|John 19:4}}). When this failed, Pilate passed his sentence and handed Jesus over to the Jewish leaders for crucifixion ({{John 19:16|19:16}}).
T

- The *crown of thorns* might have come from a date palm tree (compare {{John 12:13-14|12:13–14}}). There are Greek coin images showing such crowns, with the stems woven and the thorns radiating upward above the crown. 

- The *purple robe* was probably a soldier's robe. It was dark red, completing the picture of mock royalty.
T

- Pilate wanted to show Jesus to the crowd, hoping they would see his injuries and agree to release him. After being beaten with a whip with lead tips, Jesus was bleeding heavily.

- Pilate again declared that Jesus was not guilty, but the crowd loudly demanded his death ({{John 19:6|19:6}}).
T
Pilate knew that a riot could happen when a man popular with the masses was executed, so he shifted responsibility to crucify Jesus to the temple leaders.
T

- During the trial before Caiaphas, the charge of blasphemy (calling himself the Son of God) was determined to be the true crime Jesus had committed (see {{Mark 14:61-65|Mark 14:61–65}}). 

- The leaders had already tried to set Jesus against Roman interests and they would do it again ({{John 18:33|John 18:33}}; {{John 19:12|19:12}}). Now they challenged the governor in different way. Pilate had to maintain peace by enforcing local law, even if it did not matter to Rome. Claiming to be God's son was not illegal. Even Israel's kings did this ({{Psalm 2:7|Psalms 2:7}}; {{Psalm 89:22-27|89:22–27}}). However, Jesus claimed to have God's divine authority, which they considered blasphemy (see {{John 5:18|John 5:18}}).
T

- *Pilate … was even more afraid*: Pilate was superstitious, and stories of gods appearing in the world were not uncommon ({{Acts 14:11|Acts 14:11}}). He sensed more than a political fight was happening, so he asked Jesus, *"Where are you from?"* Pilate was not asking where Jesus was born. He was asking if Jesus was a divine man who came down from heaven. 

- Why Jesus did not answer is uncertain. Perhaps Pilate would not have understood that true power comes only from God, who had empowered Jesus (compare {{John 19:11|John 19:11}}).
T

*You would have no authority over Me*: Pilate had the power to crucify Jesus, but only because God gave him this temporary power. He allowed Pilate to have this power so that Jesus could advance toward the cross (see {{John 10:18|10:18}}).
T

- Pilate tried to release Jesus each time they talked. Despite his efforts, he failed. 

- *friend of Caesar*: This was an official title for those, like senators, who showed great loyalty to the Roman emperor. The Jewish religious leaders implied they would damage Pilate's career by claiming he did not support Rome's interests. They probably knew that Pilate was also having a personal crisis.

Pilate’s patron in Rome, Sejanus, was the chief administrator of the empire under Tiberius Caesar. Sejanus had fallen from favor and was executed in AD 31. Pilate had every reason to be afraid.
T

- Pilate sat on the governor’s judgment seat to give his verdict. In Greek, the word for this *seat* is *bēma *(compare {{Acts 25:6|Acts 25:6}}, “seat in court”).

- The Stone Pavement was the platform for the judgment seat. From there, Pilate spoke with the authority of his office.
T

*The day of Preparation for the Passover*: Here, *Passover* refers to the entire Feast of Unleavened Bread, not just the Jewish Passover meal from the night before. It was Friday, the preparation day for the Passover Sabbath. The Sabbath would start when the sun set (compare {{Mark 15:42|Mark 15:42}}; {{Luke 23:54|Luke 23:54}}).
T

The final words of the priests, “*We have no king but Caesar*,” are a contradiction of the Old Testament belief that God was Israel’s king (compare {{Judges 8:23|Judges 8:23}}; {{1 Samuel 8:7|1 Samuel 8:7}}; {{1 Samuel 10:19|10:19}}). Jerusalem and its religious leaders were killing their true king while honoring Caesar, the pagan king of Rome ({{John 18:37|John 18:37}}).
T

*Pilate handed Jesus over *to the Roman soldiers. They prepared him for crucifixion with a second flogging, which nearly killed him ({{Mark 15:15|Mark 15:15}}). Jesus bled heavily, and his clothes were soaked in blood. The crown of thorns pressed deeply into his head. Nearly in shock, the soldiers forced Jesus to march to a site outside the city.
T

- The vertical beam (Latin *staticulum*) of the cross usually stayed at the crucifixion site. The victim carried only the heavy *cross* beam (Latin *patibulum*). 

- Crucifixions were public executions near major roads. The Romans designed them to shock and warn the people. 

- *The Place of the Skull* (Hebrew and Aramaic *Golgotha*; Latin *calvariae,* “Calvary”): Most archaeologists agree that the crucifixion of Jesus happened at the site of the modern Church of the Holy Sepulchre. This is in the Christian Quarter of the old walled city of Jerusalem. 

An alternative site, Gordon’s Calvary (north of the Damascus Gate), shows what the scene might have looked like. However, it only has a tomb from the 500s BC, so it is unlikely to be where Jesus was crucified and buried.
B

The sign above the cross was written in three important languages of Jesus’ time. It announced to the world that Jesus was the King of the Jews. For Pilate, this was a way of making fun of Jesus. Pilate didn’t realise that the sign said who Jesus really is.

For those who loved Jesus, it was very painful to watch him die. Jesus’ mother was there. He spoke to her kindly. Jesus made sure that she would be cared for when he was gone.

Many things about the way Jesus died fulfilled Scriptures from long ago. This included his clothes, his bones and being pierced by the spear. To make sure Jesus was dead, a soldier stuck his spear into Jesus’ side. The prophet Zechariah had talked about this (Zechariah 12:10 – 13:1). Blood and water flowed out of Jesus like a fountain. Zechariah had said that this fountain would wash away people’s sin.
T

None of the writers of the Gospels focus on the details of being nailed to the cross because people already knew it was horrible. The soldiers used the cross as a tool for torture. They wanted victims to live for a while, sometimes for days. 

Because the Sabbath would begin when the sun set, they sped up the crucifixion of Jesus ({{John 19:31|19:31}}). Jesus had been severely beaten with whips tipped with stone or metal, so his back was deeply cut, and he was bleeding heavily.
T

Pilate posted a sign on the cross. Roman soldiers usually provided a written notice of the criminal’s name and crimes. As a possible act of revenge against the Jewish high council, Pilate ordered the sign to identify Jesus of Nazareth as the King of the Jews. The sign was posted in three languages for the whole world to understand.
T
As was their common practice, the Roman soldiers divided his clothes. The soldiers gambled for his valuable robe, which was seamless, rather than dividing it up.
T

- This is the only reference to the sister of the mother of Jesus in the New Testament. She might have been the wife of Zebedee and the mother of James and John (compare {{Matthew 27:56|Matthew 27:56}}). This would make Jesus and John cousins. If so, it would help explain why Jesus asked the disciple he loved (John) to care for Mary (John’s aunt). 

- This is the only place that mentions Mary, the wife of Clopas. She might be the same as Mary, the mother of James and Joseph (compare {{Matthew 27:56|Matthew 27:56}}). 

- Jesus healed Mary Magdalene, a woman from the village of Magdala ({{Mark 16:9|Mark 16:9}}; {{Luke 8:2|Luke 8:2}}). 

- *Woman *was a respectful and polite way of speaking in that culture (see {{John 2:4|John 2:4}}).
T

*Here is your mother*: Jesus used a Jewish family law to assign one person's care to another. This scene had additional importance: The people present represented the new community of the church that was born at the cross. Jesus wanted them to care for each other, following his command to love one another ({{John 13:34|13:34}}; {{John 15:12|15:12}}, {{John 15:17|17}}).
T

In Egypt, people used the hyssop bush to apply lamb's blood on door posts and its upper threshold (lintel) during the first Passover ({{Exodus 12:22|Exodus 12:22}}). Jesus is God's Passover lamb, and his blood also saves ({{John 1:29|John 1:29}}, {{John 1:36|36}}).
T
Jesus called out in triumph and exhaustion that he had finished the work he set out to do. On the cross he was not a victim, but a servant doing God’s bidding.
T

The Jewish authorities, eager to complete the crucifixion before Sabbath began at dusk, asked Pilate to break the legs of the men. It was common to break the legs of those crucified with a tool. It caused them to stop breathing and bleed excessively because the victim could not push themselves up to breathe.
T

- To confirm that Jesus was dead, a Roman soldier stabbed his side with a spear. 

- *blood and water flowed out*: This has several levels of meaning: 

- The spear probably cut through the *pericardium*, the sack around the heart, releasing these fluids. 

- John might have been thinking of more Passover symbolism. The Passover lamb’s blood had to flow as it died. 

- The water flowing from the side of Jesus is similar to the language of "living water" that Jesus had mentioned earlier (see {{John 4:10-14|4:10–14}}; {{John 7:37-39|7:37–39}}).
T

John stood at the foot of the cross ({{John 19:26|19:26}}). He did not just collect stories about Jesus. He witnessed the events and gave an accurate account of the life of Jesus (see {{John 21:24|21:24}}). This same confidence is also evident in the opening words of John's first letter ({{1 John 1:1-4|1 John 1:1–4}}).
T

*"Not one of His bones will be broken"*: God did not allow for the Passover lamb to have broken bones ({{Exodus 12:46|Exodus 12:46}}; {{Numbers 9:12|Numbers 9:12}}). Jesus was the final Passover lamb (compare {{Psalm 34:20|Psalm 34:20}}; see also {{1 Corinthians 5:7|1 Corinthians 5:7}}).
T
*“They will look on the One they have pierced”*: {{Zechariah 12:10|Zechariah 12:10}} describes how Israel would look on a prophet or the Messiah and lament their own tragic lack of faith.
T

- According to Luke's Gospel, Joseph of Arimathea was a brave man "waiting for the kingdom of God" ({{Luke 23:50-51|Luke 23:50–51}}). He was a wealthy and influential leader in Jerusalem and a member of the Jewish high council ({{Matthew 27:57|Matthew 27:57}}; {{Mark 15:43|Mark 15:43}}). He disagreed with the decision to kill Jesus. He asked Pilate for permission to bury Jesus in his own tomb.

- Joseph was a secret disciple (compare {{John 12:42-43|John 12:42–43}}). But his bold action showed his public support for Jesus.
B

Jewish rulers and leaders had strongly opposed Jesus. This made many people afraid to admit out loud that they believed in Jesus.

That had happened with Joseph. He was part of the Sanhedrin. He had quietly become a follower of Jesus.

But together with Nicodemus he boldly showed his love for Jesus after he died. Both men took tender care of Jesus’ dead body.
T

- Nicodemus (see {{John 3:1|3:1}}; {{John 7:50|7:50}}) was a member of the Jewish high council. He knew these bodies had to be buried before the Sabbath ({{John 19:31|19:31}}, {{John 19:42|42}}). His public support, like that of Joseph of Arimathea, might show he was becoming a disciple (see study note on 7:49–51). 

- *Myrrh* was a commonly used powder that smelled good.

- The* aloes *were fragrant powdered sandalwood often used as perfume. 

- *seventy-five pounds*: This large amount of spices was fit for royalty. Jesus, the king, received a royal burial.
T
*a new tomb*: People have discovered more than 900 first-century burial tombs in Judea, carved into the limestone hills.
T

*because it was the Jewish day of Preparation*: See study note on 19:14. It was almost the Sabbath, so Joseph and Nicodemus planned to return later to finish the burial process ({{John 19:38-39|19:38–39}}).
T

- Mary Magdalene, a dedicated follower of Jesus, went to the tomb to help finish burying Jesus (see {{Matthew 27:55-56|Matthew 27:55–56}}; {{Luke 8:1-3|Luke 8:1–3}}; see {{John 19:42|John 19:42}}). 

- Many Judean tombs were sealed with a rolling stone.
B

The day of Jesus’ resurrection wasn’t like the first day in a regular week. It was a new and special first day. It was the first day of Jesus being raised from the dead. This meant it was the first day of something new for the whole world.

Jesus’ resurrection brought life into the world that death could never destroy. This was different from when Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead. Others had to take the cloth and linen from Lazarus’ body. And Lazarus would die again later. But Jesus didn’t need anyone to take off his burial cloths. And he will never die again.

Peter didn’t understand what the empty tomb meant. The other disciple with him was John. John saw the way the cloths were lying in the grave. He didn’t understand what had happened. But he believed that Jesus had risen from the dead.

Mary Magdalene was sad and confused about everything. She was sure that Jesus was still dead. She was sure even when the angel asked her about her sadness. She was sure until she heard Jesus call her name. Jesus gave Mary a message to share. His God and Father is the God and Father of all who believe in him! Mary was full of joy. She was the first person to spread the wonderful news. Jesus is alive!
T
Mary Magdalene ran to find Simon Peter. She assumed that someone had taken the body of Jesus from the tomb. This kind of tomb disturbance did happen in the ancient world.
T

The other disciple was likely John, "the one whom Jesus loved" and the author of this Gospel (see {{John 13:23|13:23}}). He and Peter confirmed Mary's testimony by checking the tomb themselves. John got there first, but Peter went in first.
T

What Peter and John found in the tomb was remarkable. The linen cloths were on the burial bench ({{John 19:40|19:40}}). Jews also used a cloth on the face for burials. They rolled it, wrapped it under the chin, and tied it on top of the head (see {{John 11:44|11:44}}). The apostles found this cloth folded on the bench. John included these details to counter any suggestion that grave robbers had taken the body of Jesus. Thieves would have taken such expensive clothes in a robbery.
T
*he saw and believed*: Even though he did not fully understand, John knew God had done this, and he realized Jesus was alive.
T

- Even though two angels appeared inside the tomb, it was still a mystery how Jesus disappeared (see {{Luke 24:4|Luke 24:4}}).

- *Why are you weeping?*: Sorrow was not the appropriate response in this moment.
T

Mary thought Jesus was the gardener. Jesus repeated the angel’s question and asked, "*Whom are you seeking?*" Jesus wanted Mary to think. At this point Mary was looking for the body of Jesus, but she was about to meet the living Christ.
T
When Jesus called Mary by name, she recognized him immediately (see {{John 10:3-4|10:3–4}}).
T

Mary thought that with the resurrection, Jesus would resume normal relations with his disciples. She was trying to cling to the joy she discovered in her resurrected Lord. But his fellowship with her would come in a new form ({{John 20:22|20:22}}). Jesus had not yet ascended to complete his return to the Father, but the process was underway. Before his final departure, he would give the Holy Spirit ({{John 20:22|20:22}}; see {{John 14:15-21|14:15–21}}, {{John 14:26|26}}; {{John 15:26-27|15:26–27}}; {{John 16:5-15|16:5–15}}).
T

Mary was the first person to see the Lord after his resurrection. She not only saw him, but also heard and touched him (see {{1 John 1:1-4|1 John 1:1–4}}). God gave this great honor to a woman whose broken life had experienced healing ({{Luke 8:2|Luke 8:2}}). In Jewish culture, this was surprising. A woman could not even be a witness in court. No Jew at that time would make up such a story.
T

- *the disciples were together with the doors locked*: The disciples were afraid that they might be punished for following Jesus.

- *Peace be with you!*: This was a common Jewish greeting (see also {{3 John 15|3 John 1:15}}). But Jesus was doing more than just greeting his disciples. He was offering the Messiah's peace and delivering the gift of his kingdom (see {{Isaiah 9:6|Isaiah 9:6}}; {{Isaiah 52:7|52:7}}; see {{John 14:27|John 14:27}}; {{John 16:33|16:33}}).
B

Jesus spent time with his disciples after he rose from the dead. The first two times, Jesus gave them a blessing of peace. His death and resurrection brought peace.

The world is still full of wars and problems. But people can live in peace with God their Father again. Because of this, they can live in peace with one another.

Jesus breathed on the disciples and gave them the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit gives Jesus’ followers the power to continue his work. Part of Jesus’ work was to free people from the power of sin. The Holy Spirit would help the disciples share freedom and forgiveness with everyone.

Thomas didn’t believe that Jesus was alive again until he saw and touched him. Then he fully understood and believed that Jesus is Lord and God. Thomas was the sixth witness to Jesus in John’s gospel.

John the writer was the seventh witness to Jesus. He wanted everyone to believe that Jesus is the Messiah and the Son of God. That was why John wrote his gospel. Believing the truth about Jesus changes the way people live. They receive the eternal life that Jesus brought into the world at his resurrection.
T

The reality that Jesus had been raised from the dead was quite clear. Jesus showed them the wounds from the nails and the spear. He did not fake death but conquered it. He was no ghost but a real man with a real body. He had been dead but was now alive. Jesus was fully human both in life ({{John 1:14|1:14}}) and in his resurrection.
T

*I am sending you*: God sent Jesus into the world to establish his kingdom. Now, Jesus is sending his disciples to continue his mission. Christ's messengers spread the truth of his words to the world (see {{John 17:18|17:18}}).
T

Jesus commissioned his disciples and gave them the Holy Spirit. The Spirit had not yet been given earlier, because Jesus had not yet been glorified ({{John 7:39|7:39}}). 

After his resurrection, the glorified Jesus gave the Spirit to his followers. This gift fulfilled many promises that the Spirit would be sent ({{John 14:16|14:16}}, {{John 14:26|26}}; {{John 15:26|15:26}}; {{John 16:7|16:7}}, {{John 16:13|13}}). It also points ahead to the Spirit’s powerful coming at Pentecost ({{Acts 1:4-5|Acts 1:4–5}}; {{Acts 2:1-47|2:1–47}}).
T

*If you forgive anyone his sins*: The work of Christ’s followers continues the work of Christ. They do not give or take away God’s forgiveness on their own. Instead, they act according to the guidance of Jesus through the Holy Spirit ({{John 15:5|15:5}}; {{John 14:31|14:31}}).
T

*Thomas*: See also {{John 11:16|11:16}}; {{John 14:5|14:5}}. Thomas was not present when Jesus first appeared. He remained full of doubt even after his friends said they had seen the Lord. Thomas wanted the same direct experience they had.
T

- *Eight days later *was the first day of the Jewish week (Sunday). This was one week after the resurrection of Jesus. At that time, people included the current day when counting forward. The appearance of Jesus on this Sunday helps explain why the disciples met for worship on "the Lord's Day" (see {{Revelation 1:10|Revelation 1:10}}). 

- *Peace be with you*: This scene was just like the first appearance of Jesus ({{John 20:19-20|John 20:19–20}}). Jesus had already heard the complaint of Thomas, and now Jesus answered directly. 

- *believe*: Jesus challenged Thomas to believe in the resurrection like the others did.
T

*“My Lord and my God!”*: This was not a shout of surprise but a statement of deep faith. It completes John's declaration of Jesus's divinity that has framed the whole book (see {{John 1:1-18|1:1–18}}).
T
Jesus speaks of the generations of Christians who, through the testimony of others, would believe without seeing.
T

Many scholars think these words are the end of John's Gospel and consider chapter {{John 21:1-25|21}} to be an addition. John's account is only a selection of the many miracles and signs Jesus performed.
T

*so that you may believe*: Some manuscripts use the present tense, showing that John wrote to encourage those who already believe. Other manuscripts read “that you may [come to] believe,” which suggests that John was helping people begin to have faith (compare {{John 1:7|1:7}}).
